extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic and philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Analysing what propositions mean by examining the kinds of names (proper vs connotative), the phenomena they refer to, and the different types of matter-of-fact asserted (existence, coexistence, sequence, causation, resemblance). Aimed at explicating how meaning, truth, and classification work in ordinary and scientific propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names convey identity (denotation only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper names have strictly no meaning; they are mere marks for individual objects and when a proper name is predicated of another proper name all the signification conveyed is that both names are marks for the same object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Hyde was Clarendon' or 'Tully is Cicero' — Hobbes' doctrine adequately explains such predications but is inadequate for predicates that are connotative. Treat proper names as labels for individuals, not as carrying attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotative (general/abstract) names derive meaning from connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of most names (except proper names and some non-connotative abstract names) resides in the connotation — the attributes the name indicates — not merely in what they denote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing propositions whose subject or predicate are connotative, look to the connotation (the attributes/phenomena signified) rather than denotation. Example: 'man' connotes attributes (bodily form, sentient life) and 'mortal' connotes the occurrence of death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth depends on conformity of import between terms (but requires explaining how they came to apply)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition is true when there is conformity of import between its terms (e.g., 'Socrates is wise' true because 'Socrates' and 'wise' are names applicable to the same person), but one must inquire how those terms came to be names of the same thing — this is not explained merely by collocation of names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reducing truth to arbitrary naming; probe the underlying facts/phenomena that make both names apply to the same subject (e.g., experience, observed attributes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes and names follow attributes; classification is not prior bookkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: General names are not marks put upon definite objects and classes are not made by listing known individuals; classes are constituted by things possessing certain attributes, and names follow those attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume framers of language pre-determined class membership. New objects are included in classes when investigation shows they possess the connoted attributes (e.g., diamond combustibility discovered empirically).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid explaining a phenomenon by something that presupposes it (tautological explanation)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a logical error to explain a thing by another notion that already presupposes it (explaining the cause by the effect). Example: treating predication as merely placing things into pre-existing classes explains classification by classification itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing reasoning, check for circular explanations where the purported account assumes the very concept it aims to explain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish verbal errors from real (factual) errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Some false propositions are uttered from ignorance of the meaning of words (verbal), while others arise from misapprehension of things (real). A person without language can form propositions mentally that may be factually false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In critique or analysis, first ask whether the error is due to linguistic confusion or an actual mistake about facts; remedies differ (clarify terms vs. gather evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions about substances ultimately rest on phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions concerning substances or attributes (noumena) are meaningful only as grounded in the phenomena by which they manifest themselves to our faculties; e.g., saying 'Socrates was contemporary with the Peloponnesian war' rests on the simultaneous series of observable facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims about 'substances' or hidden causes, examine the observable phenomena that justify asserting coexistence, sequence, or causation between them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-fold classification of matters-of-fact: Existence, Coexistence, Sequence, Causation, Resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: Every matter-of-fact (proposition asserting matter-of-fact) affirms or denies one of: Existence, Coexistence (Order in Place / simultaneousness), Sequence (Order in Time), Causation, or Resemblance. This five-fold division is exhaustive for things that can be believed or questioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to classify the kind of claim a proposition makes; this helps determine what evidence or reasoning is appropriate to support or refute it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence (as a distinct kind of assertion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some propositions assert simple existence of a noumenon or cause; asserting existence of a noumenon is, effectively, asserting causation since a noumenon is known only as a cause of phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat existence-claims as claims about the presence of causes or entities that manifest by phenomena; require appropriate evidential grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coexistence (Order in Place / simultaneousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions can assert that two phenomena (or noumena) coexist or occur together (order in place or simultaneousness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims of coexistence by checking if the phenomena are observed together and whether their connoted attributes overlap as asserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence (Order in Time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions may assert succession — that one phenomenon follows another (order in time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sequence-claims by temporal evidence, repeated observation, and consideration of whether connoted attributes imply temporal relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation as a distinct assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Causation is a particular kind of assertion (related to existence of noumena) that claims a causal relation between phenomena or between noumena and phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat causal claims provisionally and examine causal evidence, mechanisms, and the phenomena that support inferring causation (see Third Book reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resemblance as a distinct kind of matter-of-fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Some propositions assert resemblance between phenomena (e.g., 'this colour is like that colour'); resemblance cannot always be analyzed into more basic parts and remains specifically distinct from sequence and coexistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that many general predications (class membership) are grounded on resemblance, but typically on possession of common peculiarities; in borderline or courtesy inclusions predication may assert resemblance only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borderline predication may assert resemblance rather than possession
rubrics_metrics.description: When a class is extended to include things with very inferior or dubious possession of characteristic properties, predicating the class-name often affirms resemblance and not strict possession of the class-defining properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such borderline cases use cautious phrasing ('is considered', 'may be ranked as') rather than positive predication; be alert to exceptions and anomalous genera/species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predication of sensations often denotes mere resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: Classes composed of simple sensations or feelings (e.g., whiteness, tightness) are founded on unanalyzable resemblance; predicating such class-names of individual feelings tells only of their likeness to prior sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For subjective sensory predicates, interpret claims as reports of resemblance to prior experiences rather than assertions reducible to further attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: To analyze a proposition, first analyze the connotations of its names
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscurity or difficulty in understanding a proposition usually lies in the complex connotation of the names composing it; once the phenomenon connoted by a name is understood, the proposition's assertion (coexistence, sequence, etc.) is usually clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In peer review or critique, resolve semantic complexity by unpacking the connotations (attributes/phenomena) of terms before disputing the proposition itself.
